bp: A language-model agent becomes useful only when it can turn a user's request into the right outside action. The outside action might be calling a calculator, searching a database, opening an API, or using a specialized tool that the model itself does not contain. This paper studies the gate between language and action: given a request and a changing set of available tools, the agent must pick the tool that can actually move the task forward. The need appears before any training method is named because tool use is no longer a small demonstration problem. Real tool logs are uneven, messy, and incomplete. Common tools appear often, specialized tools appear rarely, some examples are only partly correct, and the tool inventory can change. TOOL-CURE is aimed at making a tool-selection agent learn from that imperfect world instead of requiring a clean, balanced classroom of perfect query-tool pairs.
wh: The hard part is that tool selection asks the model to learn a moving map between user intent and tool capability. A user query may not use the same words as the tool description, and a tool may be rare enough that the training data contains only a few examples. The abstract says the data follow a long-tail pattern: a few tools dominate while many specialized tools are scarce. It also says some examples contain logic conflicts between the user query and available tools, and some samples are partially correct or dirty. That means the training signal is not just small; it can be misleading. Standard supervised fine-tuning treats every labeled example as if it were ground truth, so bad labels teach bad habits. Plain reward-based learning tries to learn from outcomes, but the paper says vanilla GRPO can become unstable when rewards conflict or when weak signals do not clearly teach which tool choice was responsible.
naive: A smart beginner would collect examples of user queries paired with the tool that was used, then train the model to imitate those pairings. This is supervised fine-tuning: show the model many labeled cases and ask it to repeat the label for similar future cases. That fails when the example pile is not trustworthy. If most examples involve popular tools, the model learns to over-choose them and under-learns rare specialized tools. If some labels are only partly right, the model copies the mistake. If tools change, memorized query-tool pairs age quickly. A second naive move is to use rewards directly, but the abstract says plain GRPO suffers from unstable updates when reward signals disagree or are too weak.
ap: TOOL-CURE keeps the reward-based idea but changes the training environment so the model is not thrown into the mess all at once. Its first move, Proficiency-Scaled Curriculum Learning, arranges learning into stages. The agent first practices on easier samples where the correct tool choice is more learnable, then moves to harder samples after it has built basic skill. The point is not just convenience; it reduces the chance that rare, conflicting, or noisy cases dominate before the model has a stable sense of what tool choice means. Its second move, Online Policy Guarding via Sample Screening, watches the quality of training rollouts while learning is happening. When samples look dirty or likely to send the update in a harmful direction, the method masks them so they do not drive the policy change. The central move is staged practice plus active filtering of bad teaching signals.
mech: The input is a real-world tool-selection training set: user queries, available tools, labels or outcomes tied to tool choices, and examples with uneven quality. The method starts from GRPO, a reward-based training rule where the model tries several actions, receives scores for how well those actions worked, compares alternatives within a group, and changes its behavior toward choices that scored better. TOOL-CURE modifies that process in two places. First, the curriculum component separates training into an easier phase and a harder phase. In the easier phase, the model learns foundational matching behavior: notice what the user is asking for, connect that need to tool capability, and avoid obvious mismatches. After that, it is exposed to more difficult cases where tools are rare, examples are less direct, or the query-tool relation is harder to infer. Second, the sample-screening component evaluates rollout quality during training. A rollout is one attempted path from query to tool choice and resulting reward. If the sample appears dirty, partially correct, or likely to produce a noisy update, the method masks it from the update. What comes out is a trained tool-selection policy: a model behavior that should choose tools more accurately and generalize better than plain imitation or unguarded GRPO.
math: The main mathematics is decision learning from feedback. The model has many possible actions, namely tool choices, and it must change the chance of choosing each action based on evidence from outcomes. Reinforcement learning is the idea of learning a behavior by rewarding actions that lead to better results, rather than copying a fixed label. GRPO is a particular way to compare several attempted choices and update the policy, where a policy means the model's current tendency to pick one action over another. The risk is that an update is only as good as the signal that caused it. If a bad sample says the wrong tool is good, the math confidently walks in the wrong direction. Curriculum learning adds an ordering principle: learn easier cases before harder ones so the early updates form a stable base. Sample screening adds a filtering principle: not every observed reward should be trusted equally. Masking dirty samples is a way of saying that some evidence is too corrupted to use. The tradeoff is learning from messy real data versus protecting the learner from noise that would bend the decision rule toward wrong tools.
dots: This paper sits in the LLM agent tool-use theme because it studies the moment where a language model stops only writing text and chooses an outside capability. It connects to retrieval and ranking because tool selection is a small ranking problem: from many possible tools, put the useful one on top. It connects to similarity because the system must compare a user's need with tool capabilities even when their wording differs. It also belongs to the reinforcement-learning family in the repo's current data, alongside papers that use downstream usefulness as the teaching signal for search, tool use, summarization, or agent behavior. TOOL-CURE's distinctive pressure is the quality of the teaching signal itself. Neighboring agent papers often ask how to retrieve a tool, call a search system, or route a task cheaply. This paper asks how to train the chooser when the historical examples are imbalanced, scarce, conflicting, and dirty.
ww: The method should help because the two additions attack two different failure sources. The curriculum addresses difficulty ordering. If the model begins with the hardest and noisiest cases, early updates may be pulled by accidental patterns: choose the popular tool, copy a flawed label, or overreact to a weak reward. Easier cases give the model repeated, clearer evidence about the basic relation between a request and a tool. Once that relation is partly learned, harder examples become less chaotic because the model has a reference point for what a plausible choice looks like. The screening step addresses evidence quality. Reward-based learning can be powerful because it learns from success, but it can also mistake dirty feedback for real success. By assessing rollout quality and masking bad samples, TOOL-CURE reduces the amount of corrupted evidence entering the update. Together, staged practice and guarded updates make the learning process less likely to amplify rare-label scarcity, partial correctness, or logical conflicts in the data.
po: The payoff is a tool-selection agent that can learn from heterogeneous real-world data instead of depending on abundant clean labels. According to the abstract, TOOL-CURE improves GRPO with proficiency-scaled curriculum learning and online sample screening, producing more stable and efficient learning. The practical capability is better selection of external tools for language-model agents, especially when the tool set is imbalanced, specialized tools are scarce, and some training cases are dirty. The abstract reports significant improvements in accuracy and generalization capability, so the claimed gain is not merely fitting old query-tool pairs but choosing tools better in cases beyond the exact training examples.
limits: The abstract does not show the datasets, metrics, or error cases, so the strength of the claim depends on details outside this input. The method assumes that easier and harder samples can be organized in a useful curriculum, and that rollout quality can be assessed well enough to identify dirty samples without discarding valuable rare cases. It also assumes the reward signal is aligned with genuinely useful tool choice. If the reward favors superficial success, the model may still learn shortcuts. Rapidly evolving toolsets remain a challenge because new tools may lack examples. The abstract reports accuracy and generalization gains, but it does not prove safety under adversarial tool descriptions, poisoned logs, or changing user goals.
